segments.text: Take a look at this expanse.
It looks like a galaxy, doesn't it?
Nodes floating in the dark like stars,
connected by a complex web of light.
But you are not looking at astronomy.
These are system lifecycle processes,
and the brilliant lines between them are
the flows of information.
This is how systems engineers map out
every single activity required to bring a
complex, successful product into the
world.
It is a lot to take in, isn't it?
But it is simpler than it appears.
Let me show you.
To make sense of this universe, systems
engineers differentiate between four main
clusters of work.
The first cluster is the technical
processes.
These are the activities aimed directly at
the product itself,
or, as engineers call it, the system of
interest,
because a system can be a physical
machine, a software platform, or even an
entire organization.
Take architecture definition, for example.
This is the stage where engineers sketch
out the possibilities.
Should a vehicle use an electric or a
diesel motor?
They select the best-fitting option, break
the system down into manageable modules,
and map out the boundaries so everyone
involved can see exactly how the pieces
fit together.
But those technical activities need
steering.
That brings us to the second cluster,
technical management processes.
If the first group builds the system, this
group manages the builders.
You will likely recognize project planning
here, which defines the timeline and the
budget.
But you will also find configuration
management.
Think of this as the ultimate memory bank.
It constantly gathers evolving data from
all other activities
so that anyone can see exactly what the
system looks like today and trace how it
has changed since the beginning of the
project.
Next, we have the background engine, the
organizational project-enabling processes.
These are the continuous activities a
company does every day, regardless of any
specific project, simply to keep the
business running.
Human resource management lives here,
ensuring the right specialists are
available to do the work.
But there is also something uniquely
engineered here,
like the lifecycle management process.
This is the activity responsible for
creating the very frameworks and models we
are exploring right now,
adapting them to the organization's
specific needs and bringing them to life.
Finally, we have a small but critical
cluster, the agreement processes.
There are only two stars here, acquisition
and supply.
These govern how the organization
interacts with the outside world,
how we properly bring things in, and how
we deliver things out.
None of these activities exist in
isolation.
When you link them together, you start
creating constellations of shared
knowledge.
Even if you pick two activities from
completely different groups, you will
likely find they are connected, either
directly or through a chain of other
works.
For instance, our company might acquire a
component from a supplier.
Once that component is integrated into the
system, the designers immediately receive
updated data about its interfaces.
Some works exchange a massive amount of
data, forming bright, direct channels.
Take a look at architecture definition and
design definition.
As you can see, they are tightly bound
together.
The architecture process does not just
hand over a static document.
It passes along continuous structured
data, such as architecture traceability.
This ensures that when designers dive into
the specifics, the key decisions they
make can be traced back to their
underlying rationale,
showing exactly why a particular element
was chosen to meet a specific requirement.
These are the system lifecycle processes.
Go ahead,
explore this universe yourself using the
3D visualization,
or dive deeper into the interactive
handbook.
The connections are yours to discover.
